failure_summary.description: Answer echoed clue words or was the wrong type: 'Treaty of Paris (1815)' for a 'his final defeat' clue that wants the person, and 'Area of a trapezoid' for a formula clue that wants the shape. 'capital cities' (a category label) was given for a list of names.
The archive line 'CLUE | a bouncer. right: Frank.' was misparsed and the contestant's name was given as the answer.
The answer carried an extra word or the wrong language form: 'radical sign' (the clue already says 'symbol') and 'Palazzo Pitti' (the clue is English, 'this Florentine palace', so 'Pitti Palace').

The agent picked a niche or non-matching candidate: 'Agua de Valencia' (made with cava) for the red-wine party drink, and a current Mississippi senator instead of the person who actually held the GOP leader post.

patch.reasoning: Steps 31-35 added a mandatory 'Type/Evidence/Check' line at the top and all were rejected, so I am not repeating that. These edits are narrow rules placed beside the existing rules they refine. (1) Archive parsing: the contestant-name trap recurred ('Eric' in step 32, 'Frank' here) and is worth a more explicit warning. (2) Referent type: a 'his/her' clue built around a named event or work wants the person, and a formula or property clue wants the owning thing as a bare noun, never a phrase built from clue words. (3) Form: drop a clue's role word (symbol/sign) and prefer the English head noun when the clue is English. (4) Candidate selection: prefer the candidate that satisfies every defining detail and that actually held the described role, over a niche item that appears only in a side sentence. No edits go in the protected SLOW_UPDATE block.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - CONTESTANT-NAME TRAP: in an archive line like 'CLUE | a lighthouse. right: Dana. Wrong:.' the answer is the text after the clue's '|' and before 'right:' ('a lighthouse'). The names after 'right:' / 'wrong:' are contestants, never the answer, and a bare first name is never an answer. Copy the archived answer in its own form, including a leading 'a' or 'the'. If a trivia page shows the clue but cuts off before any answer, it gives no answer. In that case pick the candidate that fits every detail of the clue, not a name from that page.

edits.target: not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - 'his / her / he / she' in a clue built around a named treaty, battle, law, deal or work ('X was signed after his final defeat at Y') asks for the PERSON behind it (the one defeated, who signed, who wrote it). Never answer with the treaty, battle or work the clue already names. A clue that describes a formula, rule or property ('add the 2 parallel sides, divide by 2 & multiply by the height') asks for the THING that has it, as a bare noun (the shape), never 'Area of a <shape>' or 'Formula for X'. A clue that is only a list of names asks for the shared entity or the specific item the passages single out, never a category label such as 'capital cities'. Test: if your answer contains a content word from the clue, or is a category label, reject it.

- When the clue says 'the name of the <X> symbol / sign / mark / term / word', give the name alone without that role word ('radical', not 'radical sign', when the clue says 'symbol'). When the clue is in English and names the generic type in English ('this Florentine palace', 'this Spanish castle'), give the standard English name with that noun ('Pitti Palace'), not the foreign-language form ('Palazzo Pitti'). The exception is when the clue asks for 'the Spanish/Italian/French name of' something, which wants the foreign word itself.

- Several candidates in the passages: choose the one whose own description repeats ALL of the clue's defining details (every ingredient, role or number), not one that only appears in a side sentence or fits part of the clue. A variant drink made with different ingredients loses to the standard item that is made with the ones the clue lists. For wording like 'popular' or 'famous', pick the mainstream, best-known item. For a clue about holding a role or office ('being GOP leader', 'chairman'), the person must actually have held that role. A different person from the same state or party who appears in the passages does not qualify.
